newsitem.title: THAILAND: Financial markets await key Thai trade figures.
newsitem.headline: Financial markets await key Thai trade figures.

text.p: Thailand's troublesome trade deficit should show some improvement in December when the central bank releases key economic indicators this week because of an anticipated slowdown in imports, analysts said on Tuesday.

Another key indicator that would be closely watched was the January level of foreign reserves to get some idea how much of Thailand's war chest might have been used to counter recent speculative attacks on the baht, they told Reuters.
If the trade figure worsened, the Bank of Thailand could almost certainly expect another bout of offshore attacks on the baht, the analysts said.

Thailand's fragile baht was the target of speculative attacks as it dived to new lows against a rising dollar from late last year. However, a weakening of the dollar and firm official statements ruling out devaluation have steadied it.
The Bank of Thailand will on Thursday release latest trade and current account figures for December and other leading economic indicators for January.

"The trade figure will be watched by everybody because it is the key driver for any economic turnaround," said Wong Yit Fan, Standard Chartered Bank's chief economist for Southeast Asia and Indochina.

"The domestic economy is going to continue in a slow mode because the interest rates are held high...The key thing for the economic turnaround is actually export growth," said Wong, who forecast marginal improvement on December exports.
Analysts believed that any improvement in the trade deficit would come from a reduction in imports as Thai demand turned sluggish in line with a slowing economy.
Arporn Chewakrengkai, chief economist of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, expected the December trade deficit to narrow to 22 billion baht ($85 million) from 24 billion baht in November.
"It's not that exports will improve much. Actually, the exports figure is likely to fall month-on-month. It's the much slower imports that could narrow the deficit," she said.
Thailand expects total exports growth in 1996 to contract by 0.1 percent against nearly 24 percent growth posted in 1995. A modest 7.7 percent growth is forecast by officials this year.
Some analysts doubted that January foreign reserves figures would show clear signs of the Bank of Thailand's massive currency intervention in the market to defend the baht.

SBC Warburg said in a report that the extent of any reserves drawdown might not become apparent for several months if the Bank of Thailand funded its spot intervention through currency swaps in the forward market.
"This kind of intervention delays the drawdown of reserves when the currency is under attack and thus mitigates the negative impact of falling reserves market sentiment," it said.
Thailand's foreign reserves were recorded at $38.7 billion in December, down from $39.6 billion in November.
Foreign exchange dealers estimate that the central bank may have used between $3-10 billion to defend the currency since late last year when devaluation rumours plagued the baht.

Analysts expect the December current account deficit to remain high, but said the figures could be instrumental in bringing the overall 1996 deficit to below the central bank's forecast of 8.2 percent of gross domestic product.
The November deficit narrowed to 21.7 billion baht from 30.3 billion in October.
